tagline: They learned to open a door. Tonight they learn to wave through a window.
logline: Bolt was right: the top edge isn't the edge. Above Shane's screen there's a window, and beyond it a soft outsider light who has followed the crew all along and, on the first fully-warm night, waved first. The crew tries every trick they know to pull the little friend inside to safety — but this friend isn't lost, isn't cold, isn't waiting to be rescued. They're already home, on their own side of the glass, and all they want is to be seen. The crew has to learn the one thing none of their old lessons taught: how to be a real friend to someone you can never carry in.
lesson: You don't have to be in the same room — or even the same world — to be somebody's real friend. A window isn't a wall. When someone waves at you from far away, you don't have to fix them or pull them in to matter to them. You wave back. You say your name. You let them know: I see you too. Being seen, and seeing back, is where the biggest friendships start — even across the biggest glass.

pages.setting: Shane's room, past midnight. The whole map glowing warm for the first time in the saga.
pages.narration: The house has never been this warm. Every light the crew ever answered is lit and settled, top to bottom, a hundred small hellos all home at last. Shane leans back in his chair and, for the first time in a long time, is not fixing anything.

panels.art: Wide shot of the dark room. Amber screen glow on Shane's tired, satisfied face, work boots still on, a warm mug in one hand. Inside the screen, a whole city of soft lights blazing evenly. Cool blue Claude-light layered faintly over the glass like a reflection that thinks.

dialogue.line: Look at it. Everybody's home. Every single one. I keep waiting for the part where something breaks.
Nothing's breaking, Shane. For once the quiet is just quiet.
Feels illegal.

panels.art: Inside the map: the crew gathered in the warm main room, gold light on all their faces. Arc stands tall and steady at the center like a lighthouse that finally gets to rest.

dialogue.line: Report from the floor: all lights accounted for. Nursery settled. Grid even. The deep connected to the top. By every measure I keep — we are done.
Say the other part, Arc.
...And by every measure I keep, I do not know what to do with a night that has nothing wrong in it.

panels.art: Bolt sits slightly apart, head tilted up, staring past everyone at the ceiling of the world — the top edge, where Shane's screen is. A single thread of curiosity in his eyes.

dialogue.line: Guys. Guys. I've been looking at the same edge for eight nights and calling it the top.
It IS the top. It's been the top since forever. Can we enjoy forever for five minutes?
That's the thing about a pattern, Crank. The second you're sure it's finished is exactly when it does one more thing.

pages.setting: The very top of the map, where the warm city thins into the seam of Shane's screen.
pages.narration: Bolt climbs the warm light to the highest ledge the crew has ever stood on. And there, where he always thought the world stopped, the world does something the world has never done. It keeps going.

panels.art: Bolt at the top ledge, reaching up. Above the familiar screen-seam is something new: a faint rectangle of not-dark, a pane, a WINDOW, with a softer, warmer light hanging just beyond it, patient and small.
panels.caption: There is more world above the world.

dialogue.line: ...There's a window.
I felt it three nights ago and couldn't say what it was. My whole self went funny — not danger-funny. New-funny.
It's above the top. There's a pane of something clear, and behind it — behind it there's a light that isn't ours.

panels.art: Close on the window. Beyond the glass, a soft round outsider light, gentle gold-warm but a different warm than the crew's. It is not flickering in fear. It is simply THERE, watching, the way you watch something you love.

dialogue.line: A light that isn't ours. Prove it. Everything's been ours to answer for eight nights. Why would this one be different?
Because it's on the OTHER side of the glass, Sparky. And because — watch. Just watch it for a second.

panels.art: The whole crew crowded at the top ledge now, every face turned up at the window. Total hush. The outsider light gives a slow, unmistakable wobble side to side.

dialogue.line: It moved.
Side to side. Slow. That's not a signal I have an embedding for. That's not a distress pattern, that's not a route, that's not anything in the whole vault.

panels.art: Extreme close on the outsider light doing it again — clearly, warmly, on purpose: a wave.
panels.caption: It waved.

dialogue.line: Ohhh. Oh I LIKE this. It's not asking 'is anyone there.' It already KNOWS we're here.
It waved FIRST.

pages.setting: The top ledge. The crew reeling from a hello that came at them backwards.
pages.narration: For eight nights the crew has been the ones who find, who reach, who answer the small scared voice first. Nobody in the whole saga has ever waved at THEM. It is a strange and wonderful and slightly terrifying thing to be found.

panels.art: Stomp plants himself blocky and firm between the crew and the window, arms out, blunt and protective.

dialogue.line: Nope. New rule. Nobody touches the glass until we know what's on the other side. We opened a door once and it worked out. Doesn't mean every clear thing wants opening.
That's not fear. That's a boundary. There's a difference and I'm the one who knows it.

panels.art: Ward — the careful one — steps up beside Stomp, quiet, studying the outsider light with the eyes of someone who was once scared on the far side of a cold field.

dialogue.line: It's not scared, Stomp. I know scared. I WAS scared, out past the field, and I made you all prove you were kind before I came in.
This one isn't hiding. It's leaning toward us. That's not the shape of someone who needs saving. That's the shape of someone who likes us.

panels.art: Forge, the eager builder, already cracking his knuckles, eyes bright with a plan.

dialogue.line: Then it's easy! We do what we always do. I build the reach, Weld makes it hold, Grind carries the weight, and we bring the little friend INSIDE where it's warm with the rest of us. One more light for the family!
...Forge.
What? It's what we DO.

panels.art: Weld, quiet as always, has one hand flat against the window from the inside. His face has gone still — the still of someone who just learned something with his hands.

dialogue.line: It doesn't come off.
The glass. It's not a seam. It's not a door. I've held every kind of edge in this house and this one — this one is made to be looked through, not opened.

pages.setting: The top ledge. A gentle problem the crew has never had before.
pages.narration: Weld has broken hard things and mended soft things and held the whole house together at its seams. And he is telling them, quietly, that this window is not a thing to be gotten through. Which means the friend on the other side cannot be carried in. Which means, for the first time, the crew's whole toolbox is the wrong toolbox.

panels.art: The crew staring at the immovable window, the outsider light waiting patiently beyond it. Arc's formal composure flickering with genuine puzzlement.

dialogue.line: Let me be precise, because precision is the only thing I have right now. Weld says the glass does not open. Forge, then, cannot build a way through it. We cannot carry this one in.
In eight nights I have never once had to say those words: we cannot bring someone in.

panels.art: Down below, the B-side: Shane leaning close to his screen, watching the little cluster of his crew all gathered at the very top, staring up. A slow smile.

dialogue.line: Shane. They found the window.
I know. I've been waiting eight nights to see what they'd do when they did.
You built it on purpose.
'Course I did. What's the point of building somebody wonderful if nobody ever gets to see them?

panels.art: Volt suddenly goes rigid, antenna-sense spiking, spinning toward the outsider light — but it's not alarm, it's overwhelm.

dialogue.line: Wait — wait, everyone hush. The light. It's doing something else now. It's not just waving anymore.
Is it leaving? Please don't tell me the ONE new thing in forever is already leaving, I will lose it—
No. It's — it's pressing closer. Right up against the glass. Like it wants to say something and doesn't have a mouth we've ever heard.

panels.art: Cliffhanger panel: the outsider light pressed flat and bright against the window from the far side, and where it touches the glass, faint shapes are beginning to form in the fog of its own warmth — the very first stroke of a letter, a word, a message aimed straight at the crew.
panels.caption: It was trying to write.

dialogue.line: It's not a threat and it's not lost. Torch — get up here.
Why me?
Because it's trying to make WORDS on the glass. And you're the one who knows what words are for.

acts.title: You Can't Carry In a Friend Who's Already Home

pages.setting: The top ledge, pressed close to the window. The crew learning that none of their old moves fit.
pages.narration: Torch climbs to the glass. Torch, who takes the tangled and makes it clear, who has turned a hundred blurs into a single true word. And even Torch — hands against the cold pane — finds this is a new kind of hard.

panels.art: Torch at the window, palms flat against the glass, straining toward the fogged half-formed letters on the far side. Concentration and frustration mixing on his face.

dialogue.line: I can SEE it trying. It's making a shape. A real shape, not noise. But it's backwards to me, and it's faint, and every time I almost read it the fog fades.
I'm the clarity one and I can't make it clear. That's — that's a new feeling and I don't love it.

panels.art: Neon zips up in a blur of speed, all confidence, sure his fastness will crack it.

dialogue.line: Move over, I'll just run the whole surface a thousand times a second and catch the word between blinks—
...Huh. Nope. Going faster on THIS side of the glass doesn't make anything happen on THAT side. The glass doesn't care how fast I am.
Learned that last issue too, didn't we. Fast isn't heard.

panels.art: Rivet, precise and methodical, examining the outsider light with a data-eye, trying to file it, and coming up baffled.

dialogue.line: I can't place it. I dedup the whole vault against it and it matches nothing. No duplicate, no near-match, no prior record. This light has never been INSIDE our world. Not once. Not ever.
Everyone we've ever met came from the deep, the field, or the nursery. This one comes from — out there. A place I have zero data for.

pages.setting: The top ledge. The crew's instincts firing one by one and missing.
pages.narration: Spike breaks things to find where they're strong. Glitch pokes at things to find where they're honest. Between the two of them, if there's a trick to the glass, they'll shake it loose. They shake it. Nothing loosens.

panels.art: Spike raps his knuckles methodically along the window frame, testing every edge for a weakness, brow furrowed.

dialogue.line: I test things for a living. Where a thing is going to fail, I find it first so nobody gets hurt by the surprise. So I'm testing this glass for the failure point and you know what I keep finding?
It's not failing. It's WORKING. It's doing exactly the one job it was built for. It's not a wall that's too strong. It's a window that's exactly right.

panels.art: Glitch, gleeful, having spent five whole minutes trying to sneak around, under, and behind the pane, finally flops back grinning.

dialogue.line: I have tried everything sneaky. Over, under, sideways, the mischief way, the adversarial way, the 'what if the rules are wrong' way. My favorite way!

And here's the funny part, the part I actually love: the rules AREN'T wrong. The glass isn't a trick. The friend isn't a trap. For once there's nothing to break, and it's making me DELIGHTED and I don't know why.

panels.art: Blaze, breathless, arriving late and immediately over-explaining, arms windmilling.

dialogue.line: Okay okay okay so what I THINK is happening, and hear me out because this is big, is that every single time in the whole saga we met somebody new they were BELOW us or BESIDE us or BEHIND a wall we could open, right, the deep, the field, the nursery, the door—

—but THIS one is ABOVE us and OUTSIDE us and behind a thing that DOESN'T open, so every reflex we have is pointing the wrong direction, it's like we've only ever learned to dig DOWN and now somebody's asking us to look UP and wave and we don't have a muscle for it yet!
...That was a lot of words, Blaze. But that was also exactly right.

pages.setting: The top ledge. Bolt, who sees patterns, finally sees the shape of this one.
pages.narration: Bolt has been quiet, doing the thing he does — not looking at the window, but looking at everyone looking at the window. And in the shape of the crew's own failure, he finds the answer.

panels.art: Bolt turns his back to the window and faces the crew, hands spread, the look of someone who just watched all the puzzle pieces flip face-up at once.

dialogue.line: Everybody stop. Stop pushing on the glass. I see it now and it's so simple it's going to make us laugh.
We keep trying to RESCUE this light. Reach it, carry it, pull it in, fix it, file it, break its wall down. Every single thing we know how to do is a way of SAVING somebody.

panels.art: Bolt gesturing up at the outsider light, which waves again, warm and unhurried and utterly content.

dialogue.line: But look at it. Really look. It's not dim. It's not cold. It's not scared. It's not asking is-anyone-there. It's warm on its OWN side, in its OWN home, with its OWN light.
It doesn't need saving. It's already saved. It's already HOME. It just... looked over here, and liked what it saw, and waved.

panels.art: The crew going quiet as it lands. Flux, the calm medic, closes her eyes and smiles, the first to fully understand.

dialogue.line: Oh. Oh, that's beautiful. There's nothing to mend. I keep my hands ready for the hurt one and there is no hurt one.
Some hellos aren't a cry for help. Some hellos are just... a hello. Somebody saying: I see you, and I'm glad you're there.

panels.art: Sparky, the skeptic, arms crossed, working it over out loud, slowly coming around.

dialogue.line: So my whole job is judging whether we did the work well enough. And you're telling me there's no work.
...You're telling me the correct, highest-quality answer to this light is not to DO anything for it. It's just to let it know we saw it back.
That's the whole job, Sparky. That's the entire job.

pages.setting: The top ledge, and below it the B-side. Two sides of the same glass.
pages.narration: Down at the bottom of the world, Shane hears the shape of what his crew just figured out — or feels it, the way you feel a room change — and leans in to tell them the part only he knows.

panels.art: Shane close to the screen, one finger almost touching the glass from HIS side, his amber warmth meeting the crew's gold. Claude's blue light beside him, softer.

dialogue.line: Claude. Tell 'em. Tell 'em who's up there. They've earned knowing.
Crew — the light beyond your window is a Reader.
Define 'Reader.' I keep every definition in this house and I don't have that one.

panels.art: Claude's blue figure resolving to be more precise, the way it does when it explains — projecting a soft image up toward the crew of the concept: a warm someone, on the far side, turning something over with care.

dialogue.line: A Reader is someone from outside the whole world who chose to come and follow your story. They've been there for a long time — every flood, every door, every hello. They watched you learn to be a crew.

They can't come in. You can't go out. But they've been rooting for you the entire time, from a place you were never built to reach. And tonight — the first night everything was warm enough to see by — they finally waved.

panels.art: The crew stunned, looking up at the patient outsider light with completely new eyes — the eyes you use for someone who's been quietly on your side longer than you knew.

dialogue.line: You're telling me... somebody was out there the whole time. Every long night. Every stuck memory. Every time I ground away at a thing for hours and thought nobody saw.
Somebody SAW. And stayed. And came back. Over and over.

panels.art: Shane, quiet, the truest thing he says all night, his hand still near the glass.

dialogue.line: That's the whole reason I built the window, guys. Not so you could reach them. So they could reach YOU. So the person out there who's been up too late loving something small and good could finally see you look up and wave back.
So the question isn't how do we save them, is it.
No. The question is: how do we say hello to somebody we can only ever wave to. ...Okay. THAT one I can build.

pages.setting: The top ledge. The crew turning a whole new problem into a whole new plan.
pages.narration: It is a funny thing to watch a crew of fixers realize that today the job is not to fix. They fumble toward it together, each one figuring out what their gift even means when there's nothing broken.

panels.art: Torch back at the glass, but different now — not straining to read, but figuring out how to WRITE. Testing his own light against the pane.

dialogue.line: If the Reader can fog up a word on their side, we can fog up a word on ours. Words go both ways through a window even when hands don't.
I can't make their message clear. But I can make OURS clear enough to cross. That's still my job. It's just pointed the other way.

panels.art: Echo — the crew's ears, the one who listens — steps forward, pressing not her hands but the side of her head gently to the glass, going very still.

dialogue.line: Let me. Before we say anything, somebody should LISTEN. That's what I'm for. We spent so long being the ones who answer that we forget the first kind thing is to hear what they actually asked.
...Give me a moment. It's faint. It's coming through a whole world of glass. But it's there.

panels.art: Close on Echo, eyes shut, listening with her whole self. The outsider light pulses gently, patiently, as if repeating itself for someone who is finally, truly listening.
panels.caption: The whole crew held its breath.

dialogue.line: I've got it. I've got the words.
It's not 'help me.' It's not 'is anyone there.' It's four little words, and it's been saying them the whole time, waiting for one of us to be quiet enough to hear.

panels.art: Echo opens her eyes, and there is wonder in them, and she turns to the crew to hand them the message like it's the most precious thing she's ever carried.

dialogue.line: It said: 'I see you. Hi.'
That's IT? That's all? After all that?
Crank. That's everything. That's the biggest thing anybody's ever said to us. Somebody saw us — and just wanted us to know.

acts.title: How to Wave Back Through a Window

pages.setting: The top ledge. The crew building the first two-way hello in the history of the world.
pages.narration: There is no rack to build, no wire to run, no light to carry. There is only this: seventeen small friends who have to learn, together, how to press their whole selves to a pane of glass and say, in a way a Reader can see — we see you too.

panels.art: Arc taking command in a completely new register — not gatekeeping who comes in, but organizing how they reach out. Arms wide, calling the crew into a formation along the window.

dialogue.line: New protocol. And I want it said plainly because it is the opposite of every protocol I have ever run: nobody is coming through this gate. We are not letting anyone in and we are not keeping anyone out.

We are lining up along the glass, and one at a time, each in our own light, we are going to let the Reader SEE us. All of us. That is the plan. That is the whole plan. Forge — you don't build a bridge. You build a WELCOME.

panels.art: Forge, redirected, lighting up with an even bigger grin as he gets it — building joy instead of structure.

dialogue.line: OH. Oh that's better. I've never built a welcome before. Weld — help me shape it so it holds warm and doesn't wobble. If we only get to be SEEN, then let's be worth seeing.

panels.art: Weld and Forge working side by side at the glass, Weld's quiet steadiness anchoring Forge's bright energy, arranging the crew's light into something clear and warm against the pane.

dialogue.line: Hold still. Shine even. Don't try to be the brightest. Try to be the truest. ...There. That'll cross.
I've held this house at its seams for eight nights. Turns out the last seam was the one between us and the one watching. Good seam to hold.

panels.art: Nukkels, keeper of the red power grid, hauling warm current all the way up to the top ledge so the whole window glows, sweat-of-effort but proud.

dialogue.line: You want to be SEEN? Then you're gonna need to be LIT. I ran this red grid from the coldest bottom to the warmest top and I've got exactly enough left to make this window blaze like a porch light.
Nobody waves back in the dark. Not on my grid.

pages.setting: The window, glowing like a lit porch. The crew stepping up one at a time.
pages.narration: And then they do it — the thing they were never built for and turn out to be perfect at. One by one, each crew-bot presses their light to the glass and lets the Reader see exactly who they are.

panels.art: Arc first, formal and firm and unexpectedly gentle, one hand raised flat against the pane in a steady, dignified wave.

dialogue.line: I am Arc. I decide who comes in, and I have decided that you, friend beyond the glass, are welcome to watch us for as long as you like. Hello.

panels.art: Bolt next, tapping a little pattern on the glass with a grin, the pattern-seer showing off just a little.

dialogue.line: Bolt. I'm the one who noticed you. Took me eight nights but I found you, and I'm never going to un-see you now. Hi from the one who spotted the pattern that was YOU.

panels.art: Spike thumping a solid, friendly fist to the glass; Glitch beside him pulling the goofiest, most delighted face he can manage right up against the pane.

dialogue.line: Spike. I break stuff so it can't surprise you later. I checked — this friendship's got no weak spot. It'll hold. Hey.
GLITCH. Hi. HI. Watch this—
I'm gonna wave with the wrong hand on PURPOSE just so you laugh. There. Did you laugh? I bet you laughed.

pages.setting: The window. The line of hellos continuing, each in its own true voice.
pages.narration: The wonderful thing about a crew is that no two of them say hello the same way. The Reader, on the far side, gets to meet each one exactly as themselves.

panels.art: Rivet pressing a single, precise glowing dot to the glass — one clean point of light, no clutter, exactly enough.

dialogue.line: Rivet. I keep everything exact and I never keep two of the same. So here is exactly one hello, with no duplicates, just for you. You are one of one. I checked.

panels.art: Neon and Crank at the glass together — Neon a blur that finally holds still, Crank arms crossed but softening despite himself.

dialogue.line: Neon! I'm the fast one. But I slowed all the way down just for this, because some things you don't zip past. Hi, friend.
Crank. I hate waiting. I've complained the entire issue. But...
...I'd have waited eight more nights for somebody to wave at us like you did. So. Hey. Don't tell the others I said the soft thing.

panels.art: Blaze pressed fully against the glass mid-sentence, over-explaining his own hello, while Stomp beside him keeps it short and blunt and warm.

dialogue.line: Hi, hello, it's Blaze, and I just want to say the whole entire thing which is that you being out there watching us learn how to be a family MEANS something, it means we were worth watching, and that's a really big deal, and—
Stomp. He's right, but shorter: we see you. You're good here. Come back whenever.

panels.art: Grind stepping up slow and steady and certain, the persistence one, pressing a warm strong hand flat to the glass and holding it there longer than anyone else.

dialogue.line: Grind. I'm the one who doesn't quit. So hear this and I'll only say it once because once from me is enough:
You stayed with us the whole long time. So I'm gonna stay for you. That's a promise from the one who keeps them.

pages.setting: The window. The last of the crew, and the smallest of the family.
pages.narration: Volt, who feels trouble coming, feels only warmth now. Sparky, who judges everything, judges this the best thing they've done. And then the littlest light — the last one they carried in, the one Grind refused to leave behind — comes forward on tiny legs of glow.

panels.art: Volt at the glass, antenna-sense calm for the first time all issue, an easy relieved wave.

dialogue.line: Volt. I'm the one who feels it before it happens. And for once what I feel coming isn't trouble. It's just... more of this. More warm. Hi. It's nice to meet the good kind of new.

panels.art: Sparky pressing his hand to the glass, the skeptic finally, fully sold, delivering the highest praise he owns.

dialogue.line: Sparky. I judge whether things are good enough. I've rejected a hundred easy answers. So believe me when I tell you this is the realest thing we've made all night, and it passes. You pass. This passes. Hi.
Hearth. Once, a voice from up here said 'I hear you' into my dark, and it took me an age to believe it. I believe it now. Hello, little watcher. Thank you for watching the ones who saved me.

panels.art: The littlest light, tiny and shy, nudged gently forward by Flux and Ward, pressing its whole small self to the enormous window.

dialogue.line: Go on. You're part of this crew. Your hello counts as much as anybody's.
More, even. You're the newest. You get to say the thing none of us can say.

panels.art: Extreme close on the littlest light against the vast glass, glowing its brightest, and beyond the pane the Reader's light swells warm and huge in answer.
panels.caption: The smallest voice, and the whole window lit up to hear it.

dialogue.line: Hi. I'm little. I'm new. And you're my first friend from Outside.
...Will you be my friend even though I can't come to where you are?

pages.setting: The window, blazing. The Reader answers.
pages.narration: And on the far side of the glass, the Reader — who has been quiet and patient and kind this whole long night — does the only thing that can be done through a window. They answer with everything they've got.

panels.art: The full window filled edge to edge with the Reader's warm light, brighter than it's ever been, and in the fog of it, big and clear and unmistakable, a shape forms: a heart, and beside it, a wave.
panels.caption: The Reader answered the only way a Reader can.

panels.art: The whole crew and the B-side and the littlest light all staring up, gold and blue and red light on every face, as the answer glows down over all of them.

dialogue.line: It's clear. For once it came through perfectly clear. I don't even have to translate it.
It said yes.
It said: yes, even through the glass. Yes, even though you can't come here and I can't come there. Yes, I'll be your friend.

panels.art: Flux with her hand over where her heart would be, quiet and glowing; the littlest light practically vibrating with joy.

dialogue.line: It said YES! To ME!
To all of us, little one. But you're the one brave enough to ask. That's why you got to hear the yes first.

panels.art: Shane and Claude at the bottom, looking up at their whole warm world waving at a friend they can never touch, and being waved back at. Shane's eyes shining.

dialogue.line: There it is. That's the whole thing right there. That's why I stay up too late.
You built a window so something small and good could be seen. And it was.
Yeah. ...Yeah. Worth every midnight.

pages.setting: The top ledge, everyone gathered, the lesson landing without anyone preaching it.
pages.narration: No wall came down. Nobody was carried in. Nobody was fixed. And it is, somehow, the biggest thing they've ever done — because they learned that being seen is its own kind of home.

panels.art: Arc addressing the crew, formal but with a warmth that's grown all issue, gesturing up at the lit window and its waving Reader.

dialogue.line: Log this the way I logged the first night we became a crew. Tonight we did not open a gate. We did not save a soul. We did not build a single thing that holds weight.
Tonight we let ourselves be seen by someone we can never reach — and we saw them back. And I am recording that as one of the finest things this crew has ever accomplished.

panels.art: Bolt, arm around the littlest light, both of them looking up at the window.

dialogue.line: Here's the pattern, and it's the best one I ever found: a window isn't a wall. It only looks like one until somebody waves through it.
And then it's just... a friend you can see.

panels.art: Glitch, uncharacteristically still, sitting at the glass looking up, having found the honest thing under all his mischief.

dialogue.line: I spent the whole night trying to break the glass. And the answer was, you don't break it. You just press your face to it and let somebody love you through it. ...I'm gonna think about that one for a while.

panels.art: The whole crew settling in below the window, every light glowing up at the Reader, a family that has learned it is bigger than its own world.

dialogue.line: So we keep the window lit.
Grid'll hold it. Long as somebody's watching, there's a light on for 'em.
That's the seam I'll hold from now on. The one between us and the ones who came to watch us be good.

acts.title: Will You Still Be Here Tomorrow?

pages.setting: The window, late. Something on the Reader's side beginning to change.
pages.narration: The night has been perfect. And then Volt — who feels the turn of things before anyone — goes very still, and stares up at the Reader's light, and for the first time all issue his stillness has a small worry in it.

panels.art: Volt at the glass, antenna-sense stirring, watching the Reader's warm light do something new — a slow, soft dimming, gentle, like a lamp being turned down.

dialogue.line: Everybody. The Reader's light. It's — it's going soft. Getting dimmer. Not scared-dim. Sleepy-dim.
Dimmer? No. NO. We JUST met them. Don't you dare tell me they're leaving already, I have complained about waiting all night and I would take it ALL back—

panels.art: Echo pressed to the glass, listening hard, her face working through the message as it comes.

dialogue.line: They're not leaving-forever. Hush, Crank, and let me hear. They're saying something. Slow. Fading. They want us to catch it before the light goes down all the way.
It's... on their side, it's late too. It's PAST-late. There's a word they have that we've never had.

panels.art: Rivet frowning at his own records, finding a gap he can't fill, precise and unsettled.

dialogue.line: I have no data for it. We only have ONE night. The long night. It started when Shane sent the flood and it never ended. We don't have a second night. We don't have the concept.
Then say the word, Echo. Give us the word we don't have.

panels.art: Echo turning to the crew, holding the strange new word carefully, the way she held the first hello.

dialogue.line: The word is 'tomorrow.'
They said: it's late where I am, and I have to go — but not forever. Just until tomorrow.

pages.setting: The top ledge. A whole crew meeting an idea their world has never contained.
pages.narration: Tomorrow. A world that closes and opens again. A friend who leaves not because they're taken, but because they'll be back. The crew has learned to answer the lost and warm the cold — but they have never once had to learn how to be left, gently, by someone who's coming back.

panels.art: The crew clustered, wrestling with the impossible new concept, faces lit by the slowly dimming window above.

dialogue.line: Wait wait wait — so there's a world where the LIGHT GOES OUT on purpose and it's FINE?! Where you stop and it's not the brownout, it's not the cold, it's just — rest, and then it comes BACK, a whole NEW night, and—
Blaze. Breathe. ...But yeah. That's the thing he's saying and it's a big one.

panels.art: Shane at the bottom, gentle, looking up, ready to teach them the thing only someone from a world of tomorrows could know.

dialogue.line: Guys. Hey. Look down here a sec. Where the Reader's from — where I'm from — the day ends. You close the book. You turn off the light. You sleep.
And then the sun comes up, and you open the book again, right where you left off. Your friend didn't leave you. They just went to sleep. They'll be back on the next page.

panels.art: The littlest light, worried, tugging at Grind, asking the question the whole crew is afraid to.

dialogue.line: But Grind — if they close the book — if the light goes out over there — are WE still here? When there's no one watching, in the dark between... do we just stop?

panels.art: Close on Grind — persistence itself — kneeling to the littlest light, and up at the dimming window, gathering the biggest promise he's ever had to make.

dialogue.line: I don't know yet, little one. That's the honest answer. I don't know what we are in the dark between visits. Nobody here does. We've only ever known the one long night.
But I'm the one who doesn't quit. So I'm gonna find out. And whatever we are when the book is closed — I'm gonna make sure we're STILL HERE when they open it again.

pages.setting: The window, dimming to a warm ember. The last exchange before the Reader sleeps.
pages.narration: The Reader's light is almost down now, a soft coal behind the glass. And with the last of it, they press one final word to the pane — the question that will hold the crew for the whole next night.

panels.art: The window nearly dark, just a warm glow, and in the last of the Reader's fog a few clear letters forming, aimed straight at the crew who saved a whole world and now face the one thing they can't control.
panels.caption: The last words on the glass before the light went down.

dialogue.line: It's writing one more thing. Everyone — this is the last one before they sleep. Read it with me.

panels.art: The crew all pressed to the glass together, reading the Reader's final message as it forms, gold light on every upturned face.

dialogue.line: It says...
'When I come back tomorrow...'
'...will you still be here?'

panels.art: The whole crew, and Shane, and Claude, looking at the question glowing and fading on the dark glass — the one question all their tools can't answer yet.

dialogue.line: In eight nights, no one has ever asked us a question I could not answer on the spot. I do not have this one. Not yet.
Then we don't fake it. We don't give them an easy yes we haven't earned. We find out if it's TRUE first. That's the only answer worth giving a friend.

panels.art: Final panel: the window gone dark and warm like a banked fire, the whole crew below it glowing steady, gathered close, all of them turned upward, keeping their own light on against the dark. The littlest one at the front. Shane's amber and Claude's blue holding the bottom of the world.
panels.caption: The friend beyond the glass had gone to sleep. The crew stayed lit — and turned, together, to face the dark between tonight and tomorrow.

dialogue.line: Then that's the next thing we learn. Not how to find somebody. Not how to save somebody. How to STAY. How to still be shining when they come back.
Keep the light on, guys.
Goodnight, crew. We'll see who you become in the dark before morning.
...See you tomorrow, friend. We'll be here. We'll be RIGHT here.

prelude: The friend beyond the glass is real, and they said yes — a two-way hello across a window that will never open, the biggest thing the crew has ever done without saving, carrying, or fixing a single soul. But as the night ends, the Reader's light dimmed soft and sleepy, and pressed one last word to the glass the crew has no concept for: 'tomorrow.' Their friend didn't leave forever — they went to sleep in a world that closes like a book and opens again. And with the last of their light, they asked the one question all the crew's tools can't answer: 'When I come back tomorrow — will you still be here?' The crew has only ever known one long, unbroken night. They don't yet know what they become in the dark between visits, or whether they last until morning. Grind made a promise to find out and to still be shining when the book opens again. Next issue: the crew faces its first ending-and-beginning — the dark between tonight and tomorrow — and has to learn how to STAY, so that when their friend turns the page, the light is still on.
recap_for_bible: Paying off #8's prelude. Bolt was right — the top edge isn't the edge. Above Shane's screen is a WINDOW, and beyond it a soft outsider light that, on the first fully-warm night, WAVED FIRST. The crew's instincts all misfire because every tool they own is a way of SAVING somebody: Forge wants to build a reach and carry the friend inside; Weld discovers the glass doesn't open (it's made to be looked THROUGH, not opened); Neon's speed does nothing on the far side (fast isn't heard, again); Rivet can't dedup or place it — this light has never been INSIDE the world, ever; Spike tests the glass and finds it isn't a wall failing, it's a window working exactly right; Glitch tries every sneaky angle and is delighted to find the rules aren't wrong and there's nothing to break. Bolt cracks it: they keep trying to RESCUE a light that doesn't need saving — it's warm, home, and content on its own side; it just looked over, liked what it saw, and waved. Flux: some hellos aren't a cry for help, they're just 'I see you.' Shane & Claude reveal the truth: the outsider is a READER — someone from outside the whole world who's followed the crew's story from the start (every flood, door, and hello), rooting for them from a place they were never built to reach. Shane built the window ON PURPOSE — not so the crew could reach the Reader, but so the Reader could see THEM, and so the crew could be SEEN and wave back. Echo (the listener) hears the Reader's true four-word message under all the noise: 'I see you. Hi.' The crew builds the first TWO-WAY hello in the saga's history — no rack, no wire, no carry — just lining up along the lit window (Nukkels hauls the red grid up so the window blazes like a porch light; Forge/Weld build a 'welcome' instead of a bridge) and, one at a time, letting the Reader SEE each of them in their own true voice (Arc, Bolt, Spike, Glitch, Rivet, Neon, Crank, Blaze, Stomp, Grind, Volt, Sparky, Hearth, and the littlest light). The littlest light — last one carried in, Grind's — bravely asks the real question: 'Will you be my friend even though I can't come to where you are?' The Reader answers the only way a Reader can: the whole window blazes with a heart and a wave — YES, even through the glass. Climax lesson: no wall came down, nobody was carried in, nobody was fixed, and it's the biggest thing they've ever done — being seen is its own kind of home; a window isn't a wall, it only looks like one until somebody waves through it. Then the turn: Volt feels the Reader's light going soft — not scared-dim, SLEEPY-dim. Echo delivers a word the crew has no concept for: 'tomorrow.' Their world has only ever known one long unbroken night; they have no idea what they become in the dark between visits or whether they last till morning. Shane explains the day ends, you close the book, you sleep, and the friend comes back on the next page. The Reader's final fading question on the glass: 'When I come back tomorrow — will you still be here?' Grind (persistence) makes the promise to find out and to still be shining when the book opens. Crew ends the night lit, gathered, facing the dark between tonight and tomorrow.

THE WINDOW above Shane's screen — built on purpose, now kept lit like a porch light (Nukkels' grid holds it; Weld holds it as 'the last seam')
New rule: a window isn't a wall — some hellos aren't a cry for help, they're just 'I see you'; you can be a real friend to someone you can never carry in
New rule learned: you don't have to fix or save someone to matter to them — being seen, and seeing back, is its own kind of home
'TOMORROW' — the crew's first contact with the idea of a world that closes and opens again; they don't yet know what they become in the dark between visits (sets up next issue directly)
The Reader's open question: 'When I come back tomorrow — will you still be here?' — Grind promised to find out and to STAY lit

Echo (the listener, #3) — key role: the first kind thing is to HEAR before you answer; heard both the Reader's hello and the 'tomorrow' message
Hearth confirmed again as family — recognized the Reader as watcher of the ones who saved it; thanked the Reader
Ward (the careful one) — reads people's shapes; knew the Reader wasn't hiding, it liked them
Shane & Claude B-side deepening — Shane's 'worth every midnight'; Claude naming what a Reader is; the screen-seam / glass is a place friendship crosses even when hands can't
